meta.title: Who really said "The best time to plan a book is while you're doing the dishes"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Christie really did plot at the sink — but this wording is a 1954 newspaper paraphrase, not her words. Her own: 'walking, or washing up the dishes.'
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The best time to plan a book is while you're doing the dishes'?
meta.ogDescription: The idea is genuinely Agatha Christie's. The sentence isn't — it started as a columnist's paraphrase in the Detroit Free Press, March 1954.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Christie genuinely plotted at the kitchen sink — she said so herself in interviews, telling Parade in 1974 that she got plots “walking, or washing up the dishes.” But this polished wording is not hers: its earliest known appearance, traced by Quote Investigator ↗, is a columnist’s paraphrase in the Detroit Free Press of March 1954 — a sentence written about Christie, not by her.

source.heading: The paper trail behind the paraphrase

docMeta.dd: A columnist’s paraphrase — not a direct quotation
“I’ve gotten others walking, or washing up the dishes.” — Parade, December 1974
No — it circulates with no source ever cited

source.excerpt: Years ago, I got some of my plots just sitting in the bathtub, undisturbed, and lining the rim of the tub with apple cores. I’ve gotten others walking, or washing up the dishes.
trail: March 1954 — the paraphrase is born. A columnist for the Detroit Free Press writes, in her own voice, that “Writer Agatha Christie suggests that the best time to plan a book is while you’re washing the dishes.” Quote Investigator ↗ identifies this as the earliest known appearance — and it is a sentence about Christie, with no quotation marks around anything she said.

1955–1962 — the paraphrase hardens into a quotation. Stripped of its context, the line resurfaces as standalone newspaper filler with Christie’s name bolted on: “The best time for planning a book is while you’re doing the dishes. —AGATHA CHRISTIE” in The Indiana Gazette (March 1955) and again in the Detroit Free Press (February 1962), per QI’s citations ↗. A reporter’s summary had become a direct quote.

1966 & 1974 — what Christie actually said. Asked by The New York Times in October 1966 when she did her creative work, she answered: “Walking or just washing up, a tedious process.” In Parade in December 1974 she was quoted directly again: “I’ve gotten others walking, or washing up the dishes.” Both are documented by QI ↗. The habit is real; the epigram is a rewrite.

Today — a quotation with no home. The line is absent from Wikiquote’s Agatha Christie page ↗ entirely, and quote aggregators reproduce it without naming any book, interview, or date — Goodreads ↗ offers only “— Agatha Christie” and concedes its quotes are community-added and unverified.
source.excerptNote: This is the closest thing to an original: Christie in her own words, quoted directly in Parade Magazine, December 1974. Note what it is and isn’t — a relaxed, first-person list of four habits (bath, apples, walking, washing up), not the tidy aphorism that now circulates under her name.
source.rightsNote: Not public domain — and not cleanly attributable either. Every documented form of this line is from 1931 or later: the March 1954 Detroit Free Press paraphrase, the 1955 and 1962 newspaper reprints, and Christie’s own 1966 and 1974 interview remarks are all in-copyright material belonging to their respective newspapers, and Christie’s writings remain under the control of her estate. But because the popular wording is a drifting newspaper condensation rather than a passage in any identifiable Christie work, we assert no definite rights status for the sentence itself. Nothing here supports a public-domain claim.

author.name: Agatha Christie
author.heading: The woman who plotted at the sink
author.bio: Dame Agatha Mary Clarissa Christie wrote 66 detective novels and 14 short-story collections, and is the best-selling novelist of all time, with more than two billion copies sold and more translations than any other individual author. She created Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple, wrote Murder on the Orient Express and And Then There Were None, and her play The Mousetrap has run longer than any other in the world. She composed much of her work — particularly dialogue — in her head before ever putting it on paper, which is exactly why the sink-and-bathtub anecdotes ring true.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in Laurena Pringle’s column, Detroit Free Press, March 1954, as an indirect paraphrase (“Writer Agatha Christie suggests that the best time to plan a book is while you’re washing the dishes”); reprinted as a standalone attributed filler quotation in The Indiana Gazette, March 1955, and the Detroit Free Press, February 1962. Christie’s own first-person phrasing appears in The New York Times, October 1966, and Parade Magazine, December 1974. Paper trail assembled by Garson O’Toole, Quote Investigator, “Quote Origin: I Got My Plots in the Tub…,” 31 July 2017.

misattribution.heading: What’s actually wrong here
misattribution.intro: This isn’t a case of the wrong name on the right words — it’s the right name on the wrong words. Christie is the correct person to think of, but the sentence attributed to her was written by someone else, about her, in the third person.

items.who: An unnamed newspaper columnist — not Christie
items.why: The line first appears in the Detroit Free Press in March 1954 as reportage, not quotation: “Writer Agatha Christie suggests that the best time to plan a book is while you’re washing the dishes.” Quote Investigator ↗ flags this earliest citation as explicitly not a direct quotation. The quotation marks were added later by other papers reprinting it as filler.

Aggregators reproduce the line with nothing but a name attached. Goodreads ↗ gives only “— Agatha Christie” and notes its quotes are community-added and unverified. It does not appear at all on Wikiquote’s Agatha Christie page ↗ — not under Quotes, not under Disputed, not under Misattributed.

“plan a book…washing the dishes” (1954), “planning a book…doing the dishes” (The Indiana Gazette, 1955; Detroit Free Press, 1962), and the modern hybrid “plan a book…doing the dishes” that matches neither early citation — all documented by QI ↗. Text this unstable is not being copied from an original.

Christie’s actual answers always gave a list — bath, apple cores on the tub’s mahogany rim, walking, and washing up. QI’s conclusion ↗ is that she described all four. The aphorism keeps the dishes and throws away everything that made the description hers.

misattribution.truthLine: She really did plan books at the sink — she said so herself, in Parade in December 1974: “I’ve gotten others walking, or washing up the dishes.” That is the sentence worth quoting, and it’s the one with a date on it ↗.

context.heading: Why this one is worth getting right
lead: This is the rare misquote that gets the person right and the sentence wrong — which makes it far more durable than an outright fabrication. Christie really did work this way. She composed much of her fiction, especially dialogue, in her head before writing a word, and she said plainly that the plotting happened during bath, walk, and washing-up. A line that captures something true about its subject meets no resistance; nobody has any reason to check it.

But the checkable claim is not “did she think this?” — it’s “did she write this sentence?” She didn’t. A newspaper columnist did, in 1954, summarising her in the third person. The quotation marks arrived a year later, added by whoever cut the line loose for use as filler. What circulates today is a journalist’s prose wearing a novelist’s name.
detailsBody: The variants give the game away. A genuine quotation tends to have one settled form; this one has never had one. The 1954 paraphrase reads “plan a book…washing the dishes.” The 1955 filler reads “planning a book…doing the dishes.” The version most often shared now — “plan a book…doing the dishes” — is a hybrid matching neither. Wording that keeps drifting is wording nobody is copying from a fixed original.

Watch out for the confident source. Because the line sounds like memoir, it is sometimes waved toward Christie’s An Autobiography ↗ — written between 1950 and 1965 and published posthumously in 1977. We make no claim either way: we were unable to search that text directly, and we will not assert a source we haven’t read. What we can say is that no one who quotes the line cites a page for it, and the earliest trail runs through newspapers, not books.

The bathtub is the better story anyway. The detail the aphorism sanded off is the one worth keeping: an antiquated tub with a wide mahogany ledge, and Christie sitting in it lining the rim with apple cores. She reportedly worked out the play Spider’s Web at the sink. The tidy version is more quotable; the real one is more interesting.
context.pull: The habit is real. The epigram is a rewrite.
